selection.method: highest remaining verified actor-primary profiles after Batch 17

profiles.name: Nanette Sargent
profiles.excerpt: Nanette Sargent became the recurring female voice at the center of Mystery House, a syndicated mystery series built around a fictional publishing company evaluating stories for radio.
profiles.bio_html:
Nanette Sargent is best documented through Mystery House, the unusual mid-1940s mystery anthology in which a fictional publishing company introduced and evaluated each week's crime story. Sargent played the female half of the framing partnership opposite Forrest Lewis, giving the series a continuing personality around its changing dramas.

The program's premise blurred publishing and broadcasting: stories were presented as manuscripts under consideration, then dramatized for the audience. Sargent's clear, controlled delivery helped establish the editorial frame before the weekly mystery took over, making her more than an interchangeable anthology player.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 30 Mystery House performances credited to Sargent. That concentrated run provides the strongest surviving record of her radio career and of her role in one of the medium's more distinctive mystery formats.

profiles.name: Penny Singleton
profiles.excerpt: Penny Singleton carried Blondie Bumstead from a hit film series into a decade of radio comedy, after beginning her career as a professional singer, dancer and musical performer.
profiles.bio_html:
Penny Singleton was born Mariana Dorothy McNulty in Philadelphia in 1908 and entered show business as a singer and dancer. She worked in vaudeville, nightclubs and Broadway musicals before Hollywood cast her as Blondie Bumstead opposite Arthur Lake's Dagwood in 1938.

The screen pairing became so successful that Singleton and Lake carried the characters into a long-running radio sitcom beginning in 1939. Singleton's Blondie balanced Dagwood's chaos with warmth, impatience and domestic authority, helping turn a comic-strip marriage into one of radio's most familiar family comedies. She later became the voice of Jane Jetson, extending a career built heavily on vocal performance.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 29 Blondie performances credited to Singleton and an additional appearance on The Abbott and Costello Show. Singing remains a legitimate second professional category because it was a substantial part of her stage and nightclub career before Blondie.

profiles.name: Alma Lawton
profiles.excerpt: Alma Lawton was a versatile postwar radio actress whose surviving work is strongest in NBC University Theater and its ambitious adaptations of major literature.
profiles.bio_html:
Alma Lawton worked regularly in American network radio during the late 1940s and 1950s, moving among prestige adaptations, suspense and detective drama. Surviving credits place her in productions that demanded more formal dramatic technique than the lighter comedy and variety programs of the period.

NBC University Theater became the strongest concentration of her work, with appearances in adaptations of writers including E. M. Forster, Graham Greene and John Galsworthy. She also worked on Lux Radio Theatre, The Whistler and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, showing the range expected of a professional repertory actress.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 NBC University Theater performances credited to Lawton, five Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances, three Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and additional work on A Man Called X, Screen Directors Playhouse, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe and The Whistler.

profiles.name: Carol Teitel
profiles.excerpt: Carol Teitel brought an acclaimed stage career and remarkable vocal range into CBS Radio Mystery Theater, becoming one of the revival series' most versatile repertory actresses.
profiles.bio_html:
Carol Teitel was born Carolyn Sally Kahn in Brooklyn in 1923 and built a distinguished career in the theatre. Her stage work included Broadway, regional companies and two Obie Awards, alongside television roles on The Edge of Night and Guiding Light.

Radio made especially good use of Teitel's vocal range. During the 1970s and 1980s she became one of the most frequently heard actresses on CBS Radio Mystery Theater, moving among contemporary women, older characters, villains and sympathetic leads without depending on a single recurring identity.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 29 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Teitel. The wider series record contains many more, making radio drama a substantial part of her professional career rather than a late sideline.

profiles.name: Glenn Langan
profiles.excerpt: Glenn Langan turned his polished screen presence into a radio leading role as crime reporter Chuck Morgan on the syndicated mystery series Stand By for Crime.
profiles.bio_html:
Glenn Langan was born in Denver in 1917 and built a career in theatre and film before radio gave him a continuing crime-series lead. His Hollywood work included major studio pictures, but the microphone allowed him to use the calm, authoritative delivery that suited reporters and investigators especially well.

On Stand By for Crime, Langan played radio newscaster Chuck Morgan, whose access to breaking police information repeatedly drew him into criminal investigations. His real-life wife Adele Jergens played Carol Curtis, giving the series a natural central partnership. Langan later traveled to Australia when additional episodes were produced there for international syndication.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 26 Stand By for Crime performances credited to Langan and three Mystery Is My Hobby appearances. The syndicated crime series is therefore the clear center of his GRH radio profile.

profiles.name: Harvey Hayes
profiles.excerpt: Harvey Hayes was a radio character actor whose surviving work is concentrated in the documentary-style crime series Whitehall 1212, with additional science-fiction and wartime drama credits.
profiles.bio_html:
Harvey Hayes belongs to the group of professional radio actors whose broadcast record is much fuller than the surviving personal biography. His credits place him in New York dramatic production during the early 1950s, particularly in programs built around crime reconstruction and suspense.

Whitehall 1212 became the strongest concentration of Hayes's work, using real Scotland Yard cases as the basis for dramatized stories. He also appeared on X Minus One and Cloak and Dagger, showing that his repertory work extended from police reconstruction into science fiction and wartime espionage.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 26 Whitehall 1212 performances credited to Hayes, two X Minus One appearances and one Cloak and Dagger broadcast.

profiles.name: Helen Strohm
profiles.excerpt: Helen Strohm became the final radio Kathy Anderson on Father Knows Best, joining the Anderson family during the program's last network season.
profiles.bio_html:
Helen Strohm was born in San Francisco in 1943 and entered professional acting while still a child. Her best-documented radio role came during the final season of Father Knows Best, when she succeeded Norma Jean Nilsson as Kathy Anderson.

Playing the youngest Anderson child placed Strohm inside one of radio's defining family-comedy ensembles opposite Robert Young, Ted Donaldson, Rhoda Williams and Jean Vander Pyl. The role required natural juvenile timing rather than broad child-performance mannerisms, helping preserve the domestic realism that distinguished the series.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 27 Father Knows Best performances credited to Strohm and two The Railroad Hour appearances. Those broadcasts document the principal radio role associated with her career.

profiles.name: Lester Fletcher
profiles.excerpt: Lester Fletcher built an international acting career that included a substantial run in Whitehall 1212 before later film and television work.
profiles.bio_html:
Lester Fletcher was born Lester Cecil Fleischman in Wales in 1922 and developed a professional acting career that eventually included radio, film and television on both sides of the Atlantic.

His surviving radio work is centered on Whitehall 1212, the crime series based on Scotland Yard cases. Fletcher's stage-trained delivery suited the restrained documentary style of the program, while later credits on The Chase and Cloak and Dagger placed him in more conventional dramatic repertory.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 26 Whitehall 1212 performances credited to Fletcher, two The Chase appearances and one Cloak and Dagger broadcast.

profiles.name: Peter Capell
profiles.excerpt: Peter Capell escaped Nazi Germany and built a transatlantic acting career in American radio, stage and film before returning to Europe in the 1950s.
profiles.bio_html:
Peter Capell was born in Berlin in 1912 and left Germany after the Nazi rise to power in 1933. He settled in the United States, worked on stage and radio in New York, and became part of the wartime and postwar repertory of European-born actors whose accents and language skills were valuable to American broadcasters.

Capell appeared in wartime dramatic programming and later became a frequent science-fiction performer on Dimension X and X Minus One. His broader career included film roles in Paths of Glory, One, Two, Three and Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory before and after his return to Germany.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves eight Words at War performances credited to Capell, six Dimension X appearances, three each on Casey, Crime Photographer and X Minus One, two Stroke of Fate broadcasts and additional anthology work.

profiles.name: Sam Gray
profiles.excerpt: Sam Gray was a durable New York character actor whose radio career stretched from Johnny Dollar and X Minus One into the repertory of CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Sam Gray was born in Chicago in 1923 and built a long acting career in New York across radio, stage, film and television. His later screen work often cast him as judges, officials and other authority figures, but radio had already given him decades of repertory experience.

Gray appeared on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar and X Minus One before becoming a recurring member of CBS Radio Mystery Theater during the 1970s and 1980s. That span links the final years of classic network radio drama to its major later revival.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 19 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Gray, nine Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances and one X Minus One broadcast. His canonical public spelling is Sam Gray; the source archive form Sam Grey remains preserved.
